video_title: The Hard Part Isn’t Buying Trend Following | Systematic Investor | Ep.426
gist: Alan Dunne and guest Uve, an asset-class-specific CTA manager, break down what trend following actually delivers inside a 60/40 portfolio: CTAs offer far more capital-efficient bond exposure than equity exposure, bond trend is the 'first responder' while equity trend is a slow 'second responder', commodity trend is the best Sharpe diversifier and pairs with bonds into an 'inflation plus 4%' defensive core, and fast trend only helps in one-month shocks. November 2026 has been tough for CTAs (SG CTA index -3.2% MTD, +10.2% YTD) on energy and bond reversals after the US midterms.

themes.theme: November 2026 CTA drawdown and macro backdrop

insights.claim: Through 11 November 2026 the SG (Societe Generale) CTA index was down 3.2% month-to-date but still up 10.2% year-to-date, and the SG Trend index was down 3.9% MTD and up 9.95% YTD, with most of the year's gains made by around May.
insights.speaker: Alan Dunne
insights.so_what: CTA benchmark context: a strong year with choppy H2, so allocators judging on recent months may misread the strategy.

insights.claim: The US midterm results flipped market expectations about Iran and triggered a sharp reversal in energy and broader commodity markets, which is where most CTAs took losses in November 2026 via long energy positions.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: Geopolitical repricing around Iran is the key driver of crowded long-energy trend positions; watch for further reversals or re-trending.
insights.quote: the midterms really switched markets expectations of what's going to happen in Iran

insights.claim: US inflation printing above expectations at roughly 3.9% annualized caused another reversal in fixed income after bonds rallied in September and reversed in October, hurting bond trend followers.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: Sticky ~4% inflation keeps bond trends choppy and the stock-bond correlation positive, undermining classic 60/40 hedging.

insights.claim: Nvidia is now large enough that its stock-specific problems project onto the broader equity market, contributing to post-midterm equity volatility in November 2026.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: Index concentration means single-name AI risk is now index risk for any equity-beta allocation.
insights.quote: Nvidia is is sufficiently large that it is projecting on the rest of the the rest of the market

insights.claim: In the last month equities fell while bonds rallied, yet bond trend lost money because trend followers were positioned short bonds, illustrating that CTA convexity is an expectation, not a guarantee.
insights.speaker: Alan Dunne
insights.so_what: Don't treat CTAs as an instant hedge; positioning at the start of a shock determines first-month P&L.

insights.claim: Uve observes enormous youth unemployment in the UK and widespread corporate cutbacks in junior hiring as firms assume AI can replace juniors, a view he rejects because juniors given meaningful projects build skills, including how to use AI in a company setting.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: Signal of weak entry-level labor demand in the UK linked to AI-substitution assumptions.
insights.quote: in the days of AI, uh people kind of tend to think that investing in juniors is not something that you should do

themes.theme: Two kinds of convexity: return vs exposure

insights.claim: Uve defines convexity as the gradient of a CTA's expected extra return to an equity move of either sign (a 'mod x' fit): a 15% convexity implies roughly an extra 75bp in the quarter for a 5% equity drawdown, and even zero convexity (uncorrelated) is valuable because most portfolio assets are a growth bet.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: Gives allocators a quantifiable way to compare defensive sleeves rather than relying on correlation alone.
insights.quote: although your book may look diversified, it is essentially a growth bet

insights.claim: Private equity, private credit, and public credit are all strongly positively correlated with equities, so a seemingly diversified portfolio of these assets falls together in an equity drawdown, whereas CTAs tend to rise.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: Private-market allocations do not diversify equity risk; true diversifiers must have zero or negative equity beta in drawdowns.

insights.claim: Return convexity (e.g., long bonds rallying when equities fall) is immediate but not guaranteed because it depends on the macro regime, while exposure convexity (a CTA mechanically turning short equities) is guaranteed but arrives with a one-to-two-month lag and initially loses money because a drawdown follows a rally when the CTA is long.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: A defensive basket needs both a 'first responder' (bonds/bond trend) and a 'second responder' (equity trend) to cover different crisis shapes.
insights.quote: So actually a CTA initially will lose money from an equity exposure convexity.

insights.claim: Equity trend helps most in protracted drawdowns but is 'too late to the party' in sharp V-shaped selloffs like the March and April (Liberation Day) Trump tariff shocks, where nearly all CTA protection came from the bond side.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: If you expect fast tariff/policy shocks rather than grinding bear markets, equity trend is a poor hedge; rely on duration or options.
insights.quote: the equity part of the convexity actually is just too late to the party

themes.theme: CTA capital efficiency: bonds vs equities

insights.claim: Because CTAs equalize risk across asset classes at about 15% vol, they deleverage equities and lever up bonds, so a 10% CTA allocation gives only about plus/minus 3.5% equity exposure but roughly plus/minus 10% bond exposure.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: Funding a CTA from bonds can add net bond exposure; CTAs are a capital-efficient bond-trend overlay, not an efficient equity hedge.
insights.quote: CTAs is a much more capital efficient when it comes to the bond sector than it is to the equity sector

insights.claim: Moving 10% of a 40% bond allocation into a CTA yields adaptive bond exposure of roughly 40% when bonds trend well and 20% when they trend badly, but the same 10% does little for the 60% equity sleeve.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: Practical sizing rule for allocators replacing part of fixed income with trend.

insights.claim: Faster trend systems commit less capital on average: a slow trend holds about 60% of full exposure in a sustained trend (about plus/minus 3.5% equity exposure per 10% allocation), while fast trend averages around 30% commitment (about plus/minus 2%).
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: Speed choice trades reaction time for magnitude of protection; slower trend gives more convexity per dollar in long drawdowns.

insights.claim: To meaningfully tilt a 60% equity allocation toward 40% via exposure convexity, an investor needs roughly a 10% allocation to a dedicated equity-trend CTA, making equity convexity expensive in cash terms.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: Equity crisis protection via trend requires large allocations; budget accordingly or use alternatives.

insights.claim: There is a historical asymmetry: bond trend provides first-responder convexity to equity selloffs, but equity trend offers essentially no convexity to bond selloffs driven by rising inflation.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: Investors worried about bond losses from inflation should look to bond trend or commodity trend, not equity trend.
insights.quote: equity trend has done nothing to you. Like literally nothing.

insights.claim: Trend following on equities alone has historically had poor Sharpe ratios (roughly 0.1 to 0.2) because value buyers create short-term negative autocorrelation (dip-buying visible in ETF flows a month after declines), whereas bond trend has been stronger thanks to carry drift, though bond trend has run at roughly a negative-one Sharpe over the past four years as bonds traded sideways.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: Dip-buying flows structurally hurt fast equity trend; recent bond-trend weakness is the exception to its long-run edge.
insights.quote: people are basically buying the dips.

themes.theme: Inflation regimes and the bond-commodity trend pairing

insights.claim: Across the 10 worst equity drawdowns of roughly 65 years, bonds hedged equities when inflation was low, but above about 4-5% inflation the stock-bond correlation turns firmly positive, as in 2022 when roughly 8% inflation sank both.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: With US inflation near 3.9%, the 60/40 hedge sits near the threshold where bonds stop protecting.
insights.quote: I think around 4 5% is kind of the middle ground.

insights.claim: Bond trend retains positive convexity to equity drawdowns across all inflation regimes, about 20% versus about 35% for equity trend, because CTAs flip positions as the stock-bond correlation regime changes; commodity and FX trend are roughly flat (uncorrelated) to equity drawdowns.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: Bond trend is the more robust defensive building block than long bonds in a positive-correlation world.

insights.claim: Commodity trend and long bonds are mirror images across inflation regimes: bonds do well when inflation is low and commodity trend shines when inflation is high, so combining them produces roughly an 'inflation plus 4%' all-weather defensive portfolio suited to pension and sovereign funds with inflation-plus targets.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: Concrete construction for liability-driven investors: pair duration with commodity trend rather than holding bonds alone.
insights.quote: the combination of commodities and bonds actually creates almost like a an inflation plus 4% portfolio

insights.claim: Equities are a growth bet delivering inflation plus 10-12% in benign low-inflation periods but barely matching inflation in high-inflation regimes, unlike bonds plus commodity trend which deliver inflation plus a roughly constant spread.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: Separate the portfolio into a growth engine (equities) and an inflation-plus defensive core.

insights.claim: With developed-market government debt around 120% of GDP, central banks and governments have much less room to cushion an equity downturn, so investors are right to be worried about downside protection.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: Weaker policy put raises the value of non-policy-dependent hedges like trend.
insights.quote: debt is now sitting at 120 of GDP, 120% of GDP

insights.claim: Uve disputes a recent Man Group paper (co-authored with Christina Hooper) that splits ~150 years of history into stagflation vs overheating regimes, arguing the splits leave too little data, pre-1970s commodity and TIPS (from 1997) data are back-filled, and equity-factor differences other than betting-against-beta lack statistical significance.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of macro-regime factor timing studies; small effective samples make regime-conditional conclusions unstable.
insights.quote: I don't think I agree with the data. I'm not sure I agree with their conclusions.

insights.claim: Industrial production, independent of inflation, reliably supports industrial and energy commodities, and US industrial production is currently up about 1.6% with rising capacity utilization; industrial production has no significant effect on trend-following returns.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: Rising US industrial activity is a tailwind for long industrial/energy commodity exposure.

insights.claim: Uve's barbell conclusion: if AI and industrial production play out, long-only copper, industrial and energy futures do wonderfully; if AI disappoints and stagflation follows, commodity trend does very well, so both outcomes favor some commodity exposure.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: Pair long industrial/energy commodities with commodity trend to cover both AI-boom and stagflation scenarios.
insights.quote: Even if the AI doesn't isn't going to play out and we're going to see stagflation, then commodity trend is going to do very well.

themes.theme: AI capex as dot-com-style infrastructure build

insights.claim: Uve views hyperscalers as infrastructure companies laying the 'pipes' for AI, analogous to dot-com telecom capex whose builders did not capture the gains; he expects the biggest winners to be cash-rich, low-capex software and application companies consuming AI.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: Favor low-capex AI adopters over capex-heavy hyperscalers for the next phase of the AI trade.
insights.quote: the people who laid the pipelines didn't actually make that much money

insights.claim: Uve acknowledges a dot-com-style valuation collapse in AI may be needed before real applications drive the economy, and that trouble financing equity-market capex could tip the economy toward stagflation.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: AI capex financing stress is a key stagflation risk to monitor alongside inflation.

themes.theme: Building a CTA basket by objective

insights.claim: Allocators should first decide what they want from trend (standalone alpha, equity crisis alpha, or bond convexity) because each objective implies a different basket; generic tools may suggest around 20% in CTAs without addressing that.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: Manager selection and sizing should be driven by objective, not by a generic diversified CTA allocation.
insights.quote: You put it into your Claude and Claude will tell you you want 20% CTAs.

insights.claim: Starting from a cheap liquid CTA core (index replicator or ETF), adding commodity trend (only 20-30% correlated to liquid trend) lifts Sharpe from about 0.6 to 0.8, while alternative-markets trend (70-80% correlated, rising as capacity tightens) adds only about 8%, and adds essentially nothing once commodity trend is included.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: For standalone alpha, commodity trend is the highest-value add to a liquid CTA; alt-markets trend fees may not be justified.
insights.quote: once you add commodity trend, it adds no value whatsoever to add alterna

insights.claim: Short-term (fast) trend programs, measured by the STTI, have struggled for standalone alpha due to short-horizon negative autocorrelation and are still 50-60% correlated to liquid trend, so they detract from Sharpe; spread CTAs offer low correlation and add modestly.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: Fast trend is not an alpha diversifier; consider spread trading for diversification instead.

insights.claim: Fast trend delivers about twice normal trend's convexity in one-month equity crises but no more than normal trend in quarterly crises, so it only pays for investors focused on very sharp short shocks; neither commodity trend nor alternative-markets trend adds equity convexity.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: Use fast trend only as a targeted short-shock hedge; don't buy commodity or alt trend for crisis alpha.
insights.quote: You're not buying commodity trend for crisis alpha.

insights.claim: A Quantica paper ('being paid to play') shows investors trend-follow their trend-following managers, with ETF and mutual fund flows mirroring roughly 60% slow-trend exposure to past performance, which destroys investor returns; diversifying across managers can mitigate that behavioral risk.
insights.speaker: Uve (guest, CTA manager)
insights.so_what: Performance-chasing allocation to CTAs is a major source of return drag; pre-commit to allocations or use multi-manager baskets.
